source_refs.note: Topic 7.3 (PDF 95-97) with the t-test and chi-square examples checked against the page images; no book figure. The decisions for both examples (critical values 2.06 and 11.07) are added, with original figures for the critical region and the die. Short Q4-6, Long Q3 and MCQs 4-7 are answered here.

blocks.text: Hypothesis testing uses a few key concepts together to reach correct decisions: test statistics, the critical region, the significance level and the p-value.

A test statistic is a number calculated from sample data that summarises how far the results are from what H0 expects. Different tests use different statistics, for example the t-value, the chi-square value and the F-value.

blocks.caption: Two test statistics
rows: x_bar: sample mean; mu_0: population mean under H0; s: sample standard deviation; n: sample size
O_i: observed frequency in each category; E_i: expected frequency in each category

blocks.text: A sample of 25 students has a mean score of 80. Is this significantly different from the population mean of 75, if the sample standard deviation is 10? t = (80 - 75) / (10 / sqrt(25)) = 5 / (10 / 5) = 5 / 2 = 2.5. With 24 degrees of freedom the two-tailed critical value at alpha = 0.05 is about 2.06, so t = 2.5 lies in the critical region and H0 is rejected: the mean does differ from 75.

So chi^2 = 3.4. It is compared with the critical value from the chi-square table for the chosen significance level (alpha = 0.05) and the degrees of freedom (6 faces - 1 = 5). That critical value is 11.07; since 3.4 < 11.07, H0 (the die is fair) is not rejected.

blocks.alt: A bar chart of the observed frequencies of the six faces in 60 rolls (10, 12, 8, 14, 9 and 7) with a dashed line at the expected 10. A box shows the working: 0 + 0.4 + 0.4 + 1.6 + 0.1 + 0.9 = 3.4; df = 5; critical value at alpha 0.05 = 11.07. A note says 3.4 < 11.07, so H0 (the die is fair) is not rejected.
blocks.caption: A chi-square test of a die (original diagram after the die example).
blocks.long_description: Even a fair die never gives exactly 10 of each face in 60 rolls; the test asks whether the differences are bigger than chance would usually produce.

blocks.text: Critical region, significance level and p-value

items: Critical region: the range of extreme values of the test statistic for which H0 is rejected. It is fixed before testing and depends on the significance level; graphs often show it.
Significance level (alpha): the largest risk we accept of rejecting H0 when it is actually true; a common value is 0.05. A lower alpha means a stricter test. It is chosen before the analysis.

p-value: the probability of getting the observed result, or a more extreme one, if H0 is true. A small p-value is strong evidence against H0, because such a result would rarely happen by chance. If the p-value is less than alpha, H0 is rejected.

blocks.text: For example, a teacher tests whether a new teaching method improves marks; H0 says it has no effect. If the analysis gives p = 0.03, then since 0.03 < 0.05, H0 is rejected: there is statistical evidence that the method improved performance. In medicine, a p-value of 0.01 when comparing a new drug with an old one gives strong evidence that the improvement is not due to chance alone. Understanding p-values helps avoid rejecting or accepting a hypothesis without proper evidence.

blocks.alt: A bell-shaped curve shows the values of the test statistic expected if H0 is true. Beyond a dashed line marked critical value, the right tail is shaded red as the critical region with area alpha = 0.05. A purple line marks the test statistic inside the critical region, and the small purple area beyond it is the p-value. A note: test statistic in the critical region (p-value < alpha) means reject H0; otherwise do not reject H0.
blocks.caption: The critical region and the p-value (original diagram after 7.3).
blocks.long_description: The two rules are the same decision: a test statistic beyond the critical value always has a p-value smaller than alpha.

blocks.prompt: A test gives p = 0.08 with alpha = 0.05. What is the decision, and does it prove H0 is true?
blocks.explanation: Since 0.08 is greater than 0.05, H0 is not rejected. This does not prove H0 is true; it only means the data did not give strong enough evidence against it.

items: Test statistic: a number from the sample, e.g. t = (x_bar - mu_0) / (s / sqrt(n)), chi^2 = sum (O - E)^2 / E.
Critical region: values that lead to rejecting H0; alpha (often 0.05) sets its size.
